[Chapter: Global Navigation and GNSS Measurements](https://jbrodovsky.github.io/advanced_navigation/chapters/05-global/global-nav.html) ## Off the lab floor [What changes when the vehicle leaves the lab and crosses the planet?]{.question} . . . ::: {.incremental} - Gravity changes with latitude and height, and its direction *defines* "down" - Gyros feel Earth's rotation, about 15°/h, on top of the vehicle's - The local frame turns as the vehicle travels: the **transport rate** - Velocity in a rotating frame picks up **Coriolis** terms - Latitude and longitude are angles: meters need radii of curvature ::: . . . Get one wrong and it enters the integrators exactly like a sensor bias. ::: {.notes} For the smartphone IMU of Project 3 the gyro bias swamps Earth rate, but a wrong gravity sign, a degree-for-radian slip, or a height in the wrong datum is never small. Where this sits in the stack: guidance needs a state that is geo-referenced (GNSS), high-rate and always available (inertial). Integration delivers all three, and because nobody checks the output by hand, integrity matters as much as accuracy. ::: ## The frame chain ::: {#20f89986 .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](06-global_files/figure-revealjs/cell-3-output-1.png){} ::: ::: $$ \boldsymbol{\omega}_{ib}^b = \mathbf{C}_n^b\left(\boldsymbol{\omega}_{ie}^n + \boldsymbol{\omega}_{en}^n\right) + \boldsymbol{\omega}_{nb}^b $$ . . . A strapdown gyro measures the sum of all three rates. Only the last one is the attitude change we want to track. ::: {.notes} ECI is the clean frame for Newton; ECEF is where satellite positions and receiver fixes live; NED carries geodetic position and north-east-down velocity; the IMU measures in body axes. The mechanization has to subtract Earth rate and transport rate to recover the vehicle's own rotation. ::: ## How far can a flat frame stretch? ::: {#4b7da318 .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](06-global_files/figure-revealjs/cell-4-output-1.png){} ::: ::: . . . The nautical mile was one arcminute of latitude, so "down" tilts 1′ per nmi: $g\sin(d/R) \approx 0.3$ mg of gravity misprojected. . . . Tiny next to a phone's accelerometer bias, large next to a navigation-grade one. The **transport rate** keeps "down" pointing down. ::: {.notes} Spherical Earth, R = 6371 km. The tangent plane rises about d^2/2R above the surface; the vertical tilts d/R radians. The tilt is the dangerous number for an INS. Book: "From Local Coordinates to Global Coordinates". ::: ## Which height did the receiver give you? $$ H \approx h - N_g $$ Mean-sea-level height $H$ is ellipsoidal height $h$ minus the geoid undulation $N_g$. . . . ::: {.incremental} - $N_g \approx -28$ m in central Massachusetts; about $-106$ to $+85$ m worldwide - NMEA `GGA` and Apple's `altitude`: mean sea level. Android's `getAltitude()`: the WGS-84 ellipsoid - Feed $H$ in as $h$: every fix tens of meters off vertically, every horizontal plot perfect - A constant offset is invisible to the innovation tests: the filter converges to the wrong height, with consistent statistics ::: ::: {.notes} "Check the datum of every height field before it touches the state." Exercise 3 of the chapter works out what the filter does with an MSL height, including the gravity error from the free-air gradient. ::: ## Pseudoranges [How do four satellites become a position?]{.question} . . . $$ \tilde{\rho}_s = \left\|\mathbf{r}_s - \mathbf{r}_u\right\| + c\,\delta t_u - c\,\delta t_s + \epsilon_s $$ . . . ::: {.incremental} - Signals from GPS orbit (26,560 km from Earth's center) take 67 to 86 ms; one microsecond of clock error is 300 m - The receiver's quartz clock is never that good, so $\delta t_u$ is an unknown - Three position unknowns plus the clock: at least **four** satellites - Each extra constellation adds one more unknown, its time offset ::: ::: {.notes} GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou, plus the regional QZSS and NavIC. Each satellite broadcasts its ephemeris, clock corrections, and health; delta t_s is known from that message. epsilon collects atmosphere, multipath, receiver noise, residual orbit and clock error. Your phone tracks several systems at once. ::: ## PVT is Gauss-Newton With $b = c\,\delta t_u$ and $\mathbf{x} = [\mathbf{r}_u^T,\ b]^T$ in ECEF: $\;\rho_s(\mathbf{x}) = \left\|\mathbf{r}_s - \mathbf{r}_u\right\| + b$ . . . $$ \mathbf{G} = \begin{bmatrix} -\mathbf{u}_1^T & 1 \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ -\mathbf{u}_m^T & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \Delta\hat{\mathbf{x}} = (\mathbf{G}^T\mathbf{G})^{-1}\mathbf{G}^T\Delta\boldsymbol{\rho} $$ . . . ::: {.incremental} - $\mathbf{u}_s$ points from receiver to satellite: moving toward a satellite shortens its range - Relinearize and repeat: the same iteration as the iterated EKF of Part 4 - Unequal variances: $(\mathbf{G}^T\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{G})^{-1}\mathbf{G}^T\mathbf{R}^{-1}\Delta\boldsymbol{\rho}$ ::: ## From the center of the Earth in five steps :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="62%"} ```{.python code-line-numbers="|2|4-5|6-7|8-9|1-10"} def solve_pvt(sat_ecef, rho, max_iter=10, tol=1e-4): x = np.zeros(4) # Earth's center for _ in range(max_iter): G, ranges = geometry_matrix(sat_ecef, x[:3]) residual = rho - (ranges + x[3]) dx = np.linalg.solve(G.T @ G, G.T @ residual) x = x + dx if np.linalg.norm(dx) < tol: break return x # [x, y, z, b], ECEF m ``` ::: ::: {.column width="38%"} ::: {#df09508d .cell execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](06-global_files/figure-revealjs/cell-6-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: :::: Eight satellites over Worcester, a 90 km clock offset, 3 m of noise: the first step alone covers more than 7000 km. ::: {.notes} The problem is so mildly nonlinear at satellite distances that a receiver with no idea where it is can start at the center of the Earth. The book's version also returns G at the solution and the step sizes; this is the bare loop. The remaining error of a few meters is what 3 m of pseudorange noise buys with this sky. ::: ## Dilution of precision $$ \operatorname{cov}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) = \sigma^2\,\mathbf{D}, \qquad \mathbf{D} = (\mathbf{G}^T\mathbf{G})^{-1} $$ . . . $\mathbf{D}$ depends only on geometry: it separates "how good are the measurements" from "how well placed are the satellites." . . . Rotate the position block into NED, $\mathbf{D}^n = \mathbf{C}_e^n\mathbf{D}_{rr}\mathbf{C}_n^e$: $$ \text{HDOP} = \sqrt{D^n_{NN} + D^n_{EE}}, \qquad \text{VDOP} = \sqrt{D^n_{DD}}, \qquad \text{TDOP} = \sqrt{D_{bb}} $$ . . . Expected horizontal error $\approx \sigma \cdot \text{HDOP}$, vertical $\approx \sigma \cdot \text{VDOP}$. ::: {.notes} Also GDOP = sqrt(tr D) and PDOP over the position block; the rotation leaves the trace unchanged, so PDOP can be computed in either frame. ::: ## Same noise, different sky ::: {.r-stack} ::: {#5be6e732 .cell execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](06-global_files/figure-revealjs/cell-8-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {#f51cce1a .cell execution_count=8} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](06-global_files/figure-revealjs/cell-9-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: ::: . . . Same 3 m pseudoranges: about 3 m horizontal error from the spread sky, over 30 m from the clustered one. And VDOP exceeds HDOP even in the good sky. ::: {.notes} 2000 single-epoch fixes per sky, black ellipse = 95% predicted from sigma^2 D^n; the Monte Carlo lands on sigma times DOP. The clustered ellipse is long and thin: all satellites lie to the north-east. VDOP > HDOP because every satellite is above the horizon, so height and the receiver clock push the pseudoranges in similar ways; that is why GNSS height is typically 1.5 to 2 times worse. DOP is a geometry statement, not an accuracy guarantee. ::: ## GNSS is not truth ::: {.smaller-text} | Source | Typical size | Typical residual | Character | |---|---|---|---| | Satellite clock, ephemeris | (broadcast values are the correction) | 0.5 to 1 m | slow, common to all users | | Ionosphere | 1 to 15 m at zenith, more at low elevation | about half removed by the broadcast model | dispersive | | Troposphere | 2.4 m at zenith, 25 m at 5° elevation | 0.1 to 0.5 m | mostly predictable | | Multipath | 0.5 to a few m; tens of m in urban canyons | not removed by models | time-correlated | | Receiver noise | 0.1 to 1 m (code) | not removed by models | nearly white | ::: . . . Not independent, not zero-mean, not white: a high-rate output is not a high rate of independent information. . . . $\mathbf{R}_{GNSS}$ too small: multipath jumps into the INS. Too large: drift goes uncorrected. Gate, adapt, and check the NIS. ::: {.notes} Orders of magnitude for a single-frequency code receiver. Beyond the budget: non-line-of-sight reception (only a reflection arrives, a positive error of tens of meters), outages, and self-inflicted timing errors: a 100 ms mismatch at highway speed is 3 m before any radio physics. ::: ## Jamming and spoofing ::: {.incremental} - At the antenna: about $-128$ dBm, $10^{-16}$ W, below the thermal noise floor - A jammer of a few watts denies GNSS over tens of kilometers on the ground - A spoofer is worse: a confident, smoothly moving, **wrong** position - Not hypothetical: ships placed inland in the Black Sea (2017); airliners spoofed over the Middle East since 2023; persistent jamming around the Baltic ::: . . . ::: {.key} Design every robot that leaves the lab for GNSS that is sometimes absent and sometimes lying. The INS is the natural detector and the fallback. ::: ::: {.notes} A spoofed position must also agree with what the inertial sensors felt; the innovation tests of the integrated filter are the first line of defense. RAIM is in the Advanced Topics part. Accuracy is closeness to truth, availability is whether it is usable, integrity is the ability to warn. A small reported sigma is an accuracy statement, not an integrity guarantee. ::: ## Why INS and GNSS fit together :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="44%"} **INS:** high-rate, smooth, self-contained, immune to jamming. Drifts. **GNSS:** global, bounded error. Slow, noisy, blockable, spoofable. ::: {.fragment} How long can the INS coast? - Navigation grade: about a nautical mile per hour - Smartphone: a kilometer within about a minute ::: ::: ::: {.column width="56%"} ::: {#8026dfbe .cell execution_count=9} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](06-global_files/figure-revealjs/cell-10-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: :::: ::: {.notes} The system is not magic: a trade between short-term continuity and long-term bounded error. The schematic is a toy constant-velocity filter; the real numbers for a phone IMU come in the error-models chapter. ::: ## Loosely coupled integration ```text IMU samples --> strapdown propagation of the nominal state <--------------------+ | | v | GNSS PVT + quality --> innovation: GNSS minus INS --> error-state update --> inject, reset ``` . . . $$ \mathbf{x}_{nom} = \left[L,\ \lambda,\ h,\ \mathbf{v}^n,\ \mathbf{q}_b^n,\ \mathbf{b}_a,\ \mathbf{b}_g\right], \qquad \delta\mathbf{x} = \left[\delta\mathbf{p},\ \delta\mathbf{v},\ \delta\boldsymbol{\theta},\ \delta\mathbf{b}_a,\ \delta\mathbf{b}_g\right]^T $$ . . . The receiver solves its own PVT; the filter never sees a pseudorange. And the nominal position is in radians while $\delta\mathbf{p}$ is in NED **meters**: that mismatch is where the first real bug hides. ::: {.notes} The five steps of the chapter: the IMU drives high-rate propagation, the receiver outputs timestamped position and velocity, the filter forms a GNSS-minus-INS innovation, the Kalman update estimates the error state, and the estimate is injected into the nominal state. This is the architecture of Project 3. ::: ## The position innovation $$ \mathbf{z}_k = \begin{bmatrix} (R_M + \hat{h})(L_{GNSS} - \hat{L}) \\ (R_N + \hat{h})\cos\hat{L}\,(\lambda_{GNSS} - \hat{\lambda}) \\ -(h_{GNSS} - \hat{h}) \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\nu}_k = \mathbf{z}_k - \hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n\boldsymbol{\ell}^b $$ . . . ::: {.incremental} - Radians to NED meters first, through the meridian ($R_M$) and prime-vertical ($R_N$) radii; corrections go back through the same radii - Add the lever arm straight to $(L, \lambda, h)$ and you add meters to radians: a bug that looks like a physics problem - A masthead antenna swings meters sideways with every roll. Ignored: a self-inflicted residual. Modeled: attitude becomes visible ::: ::: {.notes} Sign convention: GNSS minus INS, errors true minus estimate. Some texts flip both; either works if consistent. The chapter checks the linearized model against an exact ECEF computation with a 2 m mast: it agrees to 3 mm. A phone that reports only speed and course gives horizontal velocity: two rows, not three. ::: ## Loose, tight, deep :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="33%"} **Loose**: position domain - Receiver PVT is the measurement - Modular, easy to validate - Needs four or more satellites - Cascaded filters: correlated errors, so inflate $\mathbf{R}$ ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} **Tight**: range domain - Each pseudorange and rate - Clock bias and drift states - Still aids with two or three satellites - Per-satellite fault exclusion ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} **Deep**: inside the receiver - INS aids the tracking loops - Narrower loop bandwidths - Weaker signals, higher dynamics, faster reacquisition ::: :::: . . . Coupling is about robustness and integrity, not accuracy. Centimeters come from the **carrier phase** (RTK, PPP). Project 3 is loose. ::: {.notes} Tight and deep coupling are comparison points only in this course; the Advanced Topics part works through the tightly coupled measurement model. A vendor who promises "centimeter accuracy thanks to tight coupling" deserves two questions (Exercise 5). ::: # Curved-Earth INS and Loose GNSS Integration {#insgnss} A strapdown INS on a spinning ellipsoid, kept honest by GNSS. [Chapter: Curved-Earth INS and Loose GNSS Integration](https://jbrodovsky.github.io/advanced_navigation/chapters/05-global/ins-gnss.html) ## Propagate, estimate, inject [What does an INS do at every IMU sample on a curved, rotating Earth?]{.question} . . . ::: {.incremental} 1. The IMU, at high rate, propagates attitude, velocity, and position 2. GNSS, at a lower rate, estimates the accumulated INS **errors** 3. The estimate is injected back into the nominal state ::: . . . Small frame and sign mistakes masquerade as bad filtering, bad data, or a cursed IMU. It is usually just geometry. ## The nominal state $$ \mathbf{x}_{nom} = \left[L,\ \lambda,\ h,\ \mathbf{v}^n,\ \mathbf{q}_b^n,\ \mathbf{b}_a,\ \mathbf{b}_g\right] $$ ::: {.incremental} - $L, \lambda$ in radians; $h$ in meters above the WGS-84 **ellipsoid** - $\mathbf{v}^n = [v_N, v_E, v_D]^T$: velocity relative to the Earth, in NED axes - $\mathbf{q}_b^n$: Hamilton, scalar first, $\mathbf{C}_b^n = \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q}_b^n)$; Euler angles only for display and initialization - Mixed frames on purpose: the local level frame's "origin" is wherever the vehicle is right now ::: . . . ::: {.aside-box} Groves writes the radii as $R_N$ and $R_E$; we write $R_M$ (meridian) and $R_N$ (prime vertical), and Groves' $\mathbf{v}_{eb}^n$ is our $\mathbf{v}^n$. Never mix formulas from two sources without checking the subscripts. ::: ::: {.notes} The mechanization follows Groves, Section 5.4, in this book's conventions: NED navigation frame, forward-right-down body frame. ::: ## Radii and rates $$ R_M = \frac{a(1-e^2)}{(1-e^2\sin^2 L)^{3/2}}, \qquad R_N = \frac{a}{\sqrt{1-e^2\sin^2 L}} $$ $$ \boldsymbol{\omega}_{ie}^n = \omega_{ie}\begin{bmatrix} \cos L \\ 0 \\ -\sin L \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\omega}_{en}^n = \begin{bmatrix} v_E/(R_N + h) \\ -v_N/(R_M + h) \\ -v_E\tan L/(R_N + h) \end{bmatrix} $$ . . . ::: {.smaller-text} | At 42.27° N, in °/h | north | east | down | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Earth rate | 11.13 | 0.00 | -10.12 | | transport rate, car at 30 m/s east | 0.97 | 0.00 | -0.88 | | transport rate, airliner at 250 m/s east | 8.07 | 0.00 | -7.34 | ::: None comes near a phone gyro's bias of hundreds of °/h. ::: {.notes} WGS-84: a = 6378137 m, f = 1/298.257223563, omega_ie = 7.292115e-5 rad/s. Moving Delta N meters north changes latitude by Delta N/(R_M + h) radians. Some references flip the sign convention of the transport rate; this one is paired with the chapter's velocity and attitude equations. ::: ## Gravity, not gravitation ::: {.incremental} - Accelerometers cannot feel gravity: in free fall they read zero; on a table, the table pushing up. That is **specific force** - Gravity is gravitation plus the centrifugal pull of a spinning planet: $\mathbf{g} = \boldsymbol{\gamma} - \boldsymbol{\omega}_{ie} \times (\boldsymbol{\omega}_{ie} \times \mathbf{r})$ - Centrifugal: about $0.034$ m/s² at the equator (0.35% of $g$), zero at the poles - The WGS-84 ellipsoid is an equipotential: normal gravity points exactly along NED down ::: . . . At the equator, $GM/a^2 = 9.7983$; minus centrifugal, $9.7644$; add the $J_2$ equatorial bulge: $9.7803$ m/s². . . . ::: {.key} Any error in the gravity model is indistinguishable from an accelerometer bias. ::: ## Normal gravity :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="48%"} Somigliana's closed form: $$ g_0(L) = \gamma_e\,\frac{1 + k\sin^2 L}{\sqrt{1 - e^2\sin^2 L}} $$ $\gamma_e = 9.7803253359$ m/s²
$k = 0.001931852652$ A free-air term lowers it with height: $\mathbf{g}^n = [0, 0, g(L, h)]^T$, positive down. ::: ::: {.column width="52%"} ::: {#738f403e .cell execution_count=12} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](06-global_files/figure-revealjs/cell-13-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: :::: . . . Height shortcuts cost 4 to 14 µg at 10 km: a phone (bias ~10,000 µg) never notices; a navigation-grade accelerometer (25 to 100 µg) would. ::: {.notes} "Close enough" depends entirely on the grade of the sensor you are trying to keep honest. Older code uses a truncated series in sin^2 L; no reason to approximate a closed form. Exercise 2 puts an INS on the summit of Mount Washington. ::: ## Attitude first Over one step of length $\tau$, $X(-)$ is before and $X(+)$ after (not the Kalman prior and posterior): $$ \mathbf{q}_b^n(+) = \mathbf{q}\!\left(-\boldsymbol{\omega}_{in}^n\tau\right) \otimes \mathbf{q}_b^n(-) \otimes \mathbf{q}\!\left(\boldsymbol{\omega}_{ib}^b\tau\right), \qquad \boldsymbol{\omega}_{in}^n = \boldsymbol{\omega}_{ie}^n + \boldsymbol{\omega}_{en}^n $$ . . . ::: {.incremental} - Right factor: the body's turn, in body axes. Left factor: un-turn the navigation frame, in navigation axes - Exact rotation-vector quaternions stay unit length up to rounding (renormalize anyway) - To first order this is Groves' matrix form, the same algorithm ::: . . . Then resolve the specific force with the **average** attitude: $\mathbf{f}^n \approx \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\mathbf{C}_b^n(-) + \mathbf{C}_b^n(+)\right)\mathbf{f}^b$ ::: {.notes} Groves' form: C(+) = C(-)(I + Omega_ib tau) - (Omega_ie + Omega_en) C(-) tau, first order in tau, and repeated application slowly destroys orthonormality. Using only C(-) resolves a whole step's specific force along stale axes, which matters when the vehicle rotates quickly (Exercise 5). ::: ## Velocity: four terms, four stories $$ \mathbf{v}^n(+) = \mathbf{v}^n(-) + \left[\mathbf{f}^n + \mathbf{g}^n - \left(\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{en}^n + 2\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{ie}^n\right)\mathbf{v}^n(-)\right]\tau $$ ::: {.incremental} - $\mathbf{f}^n$: everything the accelerometers feel (thrust, tires, lift, the road) - $\mathbf{g}^n$: what they cannot. At rest, $\mathbf{f}^n = [0, 0, -g]^T$ and the two cancel - $-2\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{ie}^n\mathbf{v}^n$, **Coriolis**: about 0.3 mg for a car at 30 m/s. Eastbound ships weigh slightly less (Eötvös) - $-\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{en}^n\mathbf{v}^n$, **transport rate**: flying level over a sphere is accelerating toward its center. Drop it and an airliner's INS believes it is slowly descending ::: ::: {.notes} Groves' equation 5.54. g already includes the centrifugal term, so none appears here. Coriolis deflects to the right in the northern hemisphere; an airliner sees eight times the car's value. Eötvös explained in the early 1900s why shipboard gravity readings depended on whether the ship steamed east or west. The down component of the transport-rate term is about 1e-4 m/s^2 for a car and a milli-g for an airliner. ::: ## Position: radians, in the right order $$ \dot{L} = \frac{v_N}{R_M + h}, \qquad \dot{\lambda} = \frac{v_E}{(R_N + h)\cos L}, \qquad \dot{h} = -v_D $$ . . . ::: {.incremental} - Trapezoidal: both velocities are known by now - Height first (latitude needs $h(+)$), then latitude, then longitude (it needs $L(+)$) - Radians per second, not meters per second - $\cos L$ is singular at the poles: polar vehicles use wander-azimuth or ECEF mechanizations ::: . . . ::: {.key} The order is not arbitrary. Attitude resolves specific force; velocity sets the transport rate and position rate; position sets gravity, Earth rate, and the radii. ::: ## Coning: never decimate IMU data :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="47%"} ::: {.incremental} - Many IMUs output **increments** $\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_k$, $\Delta\mathbf{v}_k$: they capture motion faster than the output rate - Rotations do not commute. A wobbling axis (**coning**) makes a naive integrator drift; the velocity cousin is **sculling** - Two-sample correction: $\boldsymbol{\phi}_k \approx \Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_k + \tfrac{1}{12}\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_{k-1}\times\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_k$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="53%"} ::: {#96c2750b .cell execution_count=14} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](06-global_files/figure-revealjs/cell-15-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: :::: Naive error falls with the rate squared, corrected with the fourth power. At 100 Hz the naive integrator drifts faster than the Earth turns. ::: {.notes} Using increments is easy: replace omega tau by Delta theta and f tau by Delta v. Navigation-grade IMUs run their coning and sculling algorithms internally at kilohertz rates and output compensated increments (Savage has the families). For Project 3 the gyro bias dwarfs these effects, but the mechanism is why you never decimate before integrating. ::: ## The stationary test A perfect IMU at rest at 42° N, 60 s at 100 Hz, through three mechanizations: ::: {#b29533db .cell execution_count=16} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](06-global_files/figure-revealjs/cell-17-output-1.png){} ::: ::: . . . ::: {.key} The perfect case must sit still. One wrong sign in Earth rate, Coriolis, or gravity and it drifts immediately: put this test in every INS test suite. ::: ::: {.notes} Perfect accelerometers read C_n^b [0, 0, -g]; perfect gyros read C_n^b omega_ie, about 15 deg/h. The two quaternion factors cancel exactly, so attitude never moves. The flat-Earth case mistakes Earth rate for vehicle rotation, tilts its vertical at omega_ie cos L, and is 19 m off after a minute. Smartphone biases (5 to 12 mg, 200 to 360 deg/h) put the full mechanization about 575 m off: Earth rate is real, but with MEMS sensors it is not what limits you. The bias is. ::: ## Leveling: roll and pitch from gravity $$ \phi = \operatorname{atan2}(-f_y,\ -f_z), \qquad \theta = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(f_x,\ \sqrt{f_y^2 + f_z^2}\right) $$ . . . ::: {.incremental} - At rest, $\mathbf{f}^b = g\,[\sin\theta,\ -\cos\theta\sin\phi,\ -\cos\theta\cos\phi]^T$ in FRD axes: two angles fall out - Average for a few seconds: noise and vibration average down. **Bias does not** ::: . . . $$ \delta\theta_\text{tilt} \approx \frac{b_a}{g} \qquad (\text{about } 0.06^\circ \text{ per milli-g}) $$ . . . Harmless while parked: the tilt leaks exactly enough gravity to cancel the bias. It shows up once the vehicle turns and the bias rotates but the tilt does not. ## Heading: gyrocompassing :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="46%"} At rest the gyros sense only Earth rate. Its horizontal part, $\omega_{ie}\cos L \approx 11$°/h at WPI, points **north**. $$ \delta\psi \approx \frac{b_{g,E}}{\omega_{ie}\cos L} $$ ::: {.incremental} - Navigation grade, 0.01°/h: a few hundredths of a degree - Smartphone, a few hundred °/h: twenty to thirty times the signal. The compass points at the bias ::: ::: ::: {.column width="54%"} ::: {#3952deda .cell execution_count=18} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](06-global_files/figure-revealjs/cell-19-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: :::: ::: {.notes} Level first, rotate the gyro outputs into the leveled frame, psi = atan2(-w_y, w_x). Ships found north this way long before GNSS: Anschuetz-Kaempfe's gyrocompass went to sea in 1908, Sperry's in 1911, both sensing the same 15 deg/h with a spinning wheel. The rule of thumb holds while the bias is small next to omega_ie cos L and then fails gracefully into nonsense: at 300 deg/h the answer is wrong by almost 90 degrees. Within a degree of north needs a residual bias under about 0.2 deg/h, so bench calibration does not save a phone either. ::: ## Where a MEMS INS gets heading ::: {.incremental} - **Magnetometer:** correct for declination (about $-14^\circ$ at WPI) and the vehicle's hard- and soft-iron distortion. A few degrees in the open, badly wrong near steel, rebar, and motors - **GNSS course over ground:** for a car that does not crab, its heading to about a degree above a few m/s. Below walking speed, noise - **Dual GNSS antennas:** heading from the carrier-phase baseline, a fraction of a degree, even when parked - **Maneuvers:** start with a large heading uncertainty and let the dynamics reveal it (the simulated drive, coming up) ::: . . . [A smartphone has no business gyrocompassing.]{.muted} ## The error state, on a curved Earth Part 4 promised this filter. Units: milli-g and micro-g use standard gravity 9.80665 m/s^2 as a conversion constant. ::: ## Three kinds of error :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="33%"} **Deterministic**: calibrate - Bias at a reference temperature - Scale factor - Misalignment, cross-axis sensitivity - Mounting-angle error ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} **Stochastic**: model - White noise (angle and velocity random walk) - Bias instability - Bias random walk - Quantization - Turn-on bias ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} **Environmental**: test - Temperature - Vibration and rectification - Magnetic sensitivity - g-dependent gyro errors - Flexure between sensors ::: :::: . . . ::: {.key} Turn-on bias straddles the line: constant within a run, so the filter can estimate it; different at every power-up, so a factory calibration cannot. ::: ## Bias wins :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Accelerometer bias**, integrated twice: $$ \Delta p(t) \approx \tfrac{1}{2}\,b_a t^2 $$ 1 mg for a minute: **17.7 m** ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.fragment} **Gyro bias**: a tilt $\delta\theta \approx b_g t$ leaks $g_0\,\delta\theta$ of gravity: $$ \Delta p(t) \approx \tfrac{1}{6}\,g_0 b_g t^3 $$ 10°/h for a minute: **17 m**, and pulling ahead ::: ::: :::: . . . **White noise** integrates too, but partly cancels: $$ \sigma_p^{\text{VRW}}(t) = \frac{N_a\,t^{3/2}}{\sqrt{3}}, \qquad \sigma_p^{\text{ARW}}(t) = \frac{g_0 N_g\,t^{5/2}}{\sqrt{20}} $$ . . . ::: {.key} Attitude is not just an output of the INS. Propagate less often (say once per GNSS epoch) and use Van Loan: the first-order formula at 1 Hz comes out several percent optimistic, more so when the vehicle maneuvers. Then tune against innovation statistics; a quiet bench data sheet often understates the noise on a vibrating vehicle by several times. ::: ## Heading hides in straight lines [What can GNSS position fixes teach the filter about heading?]{.accent} $$ \delta\dot{\mathbf{v}} = -[\hat{\mathbf{f}}^n]_\times\delta\boldsymbol{\theta} - \hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n\delta\mathbf{b}_a $$ . . . Straight, level, constant speed: $\hat{\mathbf{f}}^n = [0, 0, -g]^T$ and $$ -[\hat{\mathbf{f}}^n]_\times\delta\boldsymbol{\theta} = \begin{bmatrix} -g\,\delta\theta_E \\ g\,\delta\theta_N \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} $$ . . . $\delta\theta_D$ is gone: no innovation, ever. Heading is **unobservable**, not merely weak. . . . Horizontal specific force brings it back; only its *changes* separate heading from accelerometer bias. ## Which maneuvers reveal what ::: {.smaller-text} | 30 s of 1 Hz position fixes | observable directions | heading | |---|:---:|:---:| | straight, constant speed | 11 of 15 | hidden | | constant acceleration | 11 of 15 | hidden | | cruise, then accelerate | 14 of 15 | observable | | cruise, 90° turn, cruise | 15 of 15 | observable | ::: . . . ::: {.incremental} - Cruising hides yaw, the vertical gyro bias, and two tilt and accelerometer-bias blends (the leveling ambiguity) - A turn rotates the body-fixed biases against the tilt and separates them all ::: . . . ::: {.key} A filter cannot learn what the motion never reveals. ::: ::: {.notes} Rank of the observability matrix of the 15-state model, stacked over 30 s of fixes, for a level vehicle. Holding a constant acceleration does not help: a constant horizontal specific force times a heading error looks just like a constant accelerometer bias. Starting or stopping an acceleration does. Vertical accelerometer bias and height error are tangled with gravity modeling and GNSS vertical quality. Exercise 3: stop-and-go without turns. ::: ## Choosing states Start with the 15. Add a state only when ::: {.incremental} 1. the error source is large enough to matter, 2. the measurements **and the motion** can observe it, and 3. you have a reasonable process model and initialization for it. ::: . . .
